title: Biomolecules: Carbohydrates, Proteins, Fats, DNA

cards.b: Your body is built from four families of big molecules: carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids) and nucleic acids. Each is a polymer or an assembly of simple units. Understanding them explains food, energy, enzymes, inheritance and disease.

General formula roughly Cx(H2O)y. Glucose C6H12O6 is the body's main fuel. Sugars join into chains:

  • Sucrose (table sugar): glucose + fructose.
  • Starch: plants' energy store, long chains of glucose.
  • Glycogen: the animal equivalent.
  • Cellulose: plant cell walls, also glucose chains but joined differently; humans cannot digest it (fibre).

Proteins are chains of amino acids (20 common ones), each with -NH2 and -COOH. Two amino acids join with loss of water to form a peptide bond.

Shape decides function: enzymes, haemoglobin, antibodies, keratin in hair. Heat or acid denatures them: a boiled egg cannot go back. Frederick Sanger sequenced insulin in 1955 (Nobel 1958).

A fat (triglyceride) is one glycerol joined to three fatty acids through ester links. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C bonds (solid at room temperature, like ghee and butter). Unsaturated ones have C=C bonds (liquid, like most plant oils).

Fats give about 9 kcal per gram, more than twice carbohydrate or protein (about 4). They also form cell membranes and carry vitamins A, D, E and K.

Enzymes are protein catalysts. They fit substrates like a lock and key (or an induced fit), lower activation energy and work at body temperature and specific pH. Amylase breaks starch, pepsin breaks proteins in the acid of the stomach.

Vitamins are small organic compounds needed in tiny amounts, e.g. vitamin C (scurvy) and D (rickets).

DNA is a polymer of nucleotides: sugar (deoxyribose) + phosphate + one of four bases, A, T, G, C. Watson and Crick, 1953, building on X-ray work by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, proposed the double helix. The strands pair by hydrogen bonds: A with T, G with C.

Three bases form a codon that specifies an amino acid. DNA is copied to RNA, then RNA is read to build proteins.

One strand reads A-T-G-C. The partner strand is T-A-C-G.

If DNA is 30 percent A, then T = 30 percent; G + C = 40 percent, so G = C = 20 percent each.

Energy: 50 g of fat gives about 50 x 9 = 450 kcal; 50 g of sugar gives 50 x 4 = 200 kcal.

• Fats are not all bad. You need essential fatty acids.
  • Proteins are not only for muscle. Enzymes and hormones are proteins too.
  • DNA does not make proteins directly; RNA does the transfer.
  • Cooked proteins are not destroyed nutritionally; denaturing makes them easier to digest.

Har Gobind Khorana, born in Raipur village (in present-day Pakistan) and educated in Punjab University in Lahore, shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for helping to decode the genetic code and later made the first synthetic gene. India's famed pulses, ghee and millets offer all the biomolecule groups: protein, fat and complex carbohydrate.

• Carbohydrates: glucose, starch, cellulose. Proteins: amino-acid chains joined by peptide bonds.
  • Fats: glycerol plus three fatty acids, high in energy.
  • DNA: double helix (1953), A-T and G-C pairing.

Think about it

1. Why can we digest starch but not cellulose, although both are glucose polymers?

2. Why does a high fever risk damaging enzymes?
